concepts.name: Policy, standard, procedure, and guideline
concepts.description: Governance documents answer different questions: a policy sets required direction, a standard makes specific requirements mandatory, a procedure gives steps, and a guideline gives recommended guidance.

concepts.name: Acceptable use policy (AUP)
concepts.description: An acceptable use policy (AUP) defines permitted and prohibited use of organizational systems, networks, accounts, and data.

concepts.name: Information security policies
concepts.description: Information security policies translate management intent and risk decisions into organization-wide security requirements.

concepts.name: Business continuity, disaster recovery, and incident response
concepts.description: Business continuity, disaster recovery, and incident response are related but distinct: continuity keeps critical business functions operating, disaster recovery restores technology and services, and incident response handles security incidents.

concepts.name: SDLC and change-management policy
concepts.description: Security governance should set expectations for the software development lifecycle (SDLC) and for controlled changes so security is considered before changes reach production.

concepts.name: Security standards
concepts.description: A security standard turns policy into specific mandatory requirements, such as password, access-control, physical-security, or encryption requirements.

concepts.name: Operational procedures
concepts.description: A procedure describes the steps people follow to perform a governed activity consistently, including change management and onboarding/offboarding.

concepts.name: Playbooks
concepts.description: A playbook is an action-oriented set of steps for a known situation, often used for recurring operational or incident scenarios.

concepts.name: External governance considerations
concepts.description: Security governance must account for obligations outside the organization, including regulatory, legal, and industry requirements that can differ across local, regional, national, and global jurisdictions.

concepts.name: Governance monitoring and revision
concepts.description: Governance is not a one-time document-writing exercise. Policies, standards, and procedures need monitoring and revision as risks, systems, laws, and business needs change.

concepts.name: Governance structures
concepts.description: Boards, committees, and government entities can provide oversight or direction. Governance may be centralized under one authority or decentralized across business units.

concepts.name: Owners, controllers, processors, custodians, and stewards
concepts.description: Security+ expects you to distinguish accountability from hands-on handling: owners make accountability and protection decisions; custodians/stewards manage or safeguard information; privacy controllers determine purposes and means of processing, while processors act on a controller's behalf.

concepts.name: Risk identification and assessment
concepts.description: Risk identification finds conditions that could harm objectives. A risk assessment then analyzes those risks so the organization can prioritize decisions.

concepts.name: Ad hoc, recurring, one-time, and continuous assessments
concepts.description: Risk assessments can be triggered ad hoc, scheduled to recur, performed once for a specific decision, or updated continuously as conditions change.

concepts.name: Qualitative vs. quantitative risk analysis
concepts.description: Qualitative analysis uses relative labels or rankings such as low, medium, and high. Quantitative analysis uses numeric estimates, often including money, probability, or frequency.

concepts.name: Single loss expectancy (SLE) and exposure factor
concepts.description: Single loss expectancy (SLE) estimates the loss from one occurrence. A common Security+ calculation is SLE = asset value × exposure factor (EF).

concepts.name: Annualized rate of occurrence (ARO) and annualized loss expectancy (ALE)
concepts.description: Annualized rate of occurrence (ARO) estimates how often an event occurs per year. Annualized loss expectancy (ALE) estimates yearly loss using ALE = SLE × ARO.

concepts.name: Probability, likelihood, and impact
concepts.description: Risk analysis considers how likely an event is and how severe its impact would be. Probability may be numeric; likelihood may also be expressed qualitatively.

concepts.name: Risk register
concepts.description: A risk register is the working record used to track identified risks, their analysis, ownership, treatment, and status.

concepts.name: KRIs, risk owners, and risk thresholds
concepts.description: A key risk indicator (KRI) provides a measurable signal about changing exposure. A risk owner is accountable for the risk decision, and a risk threshold is a boundary that can trigger action or escalation.

concepts.name: Risk appetite vs. risk tolerance
concepts.description: Risk appetite is the broad amount and type of risk an organization is willing to pursue or retain. Risk tolerance is the acceptable variation or limit around a specific objective or activity.

concepts.name: Expansionary, conservative, and neutral risk appetite
concepts.description: Security+ describes risk appetite as expansionary, conservative, or neutral. Expansionary accepts more risk for opportunity, conservative favors lower exposure, and neutral aims for a balanced posture.

concepts.name: Transfer, accept, avoid, and mitigate
concepts.description: Four core risk strategies are transfer, accept, avoid, and mitigate. The right choice depends on business objectives, cost, feasibility, and residual risk.

concepts.name: Exceptions and exemptions
concepts.description: Exceptions and exemptions are approved departures from a normal requirement. Exact terminology varies by organization, but Security+ expects controlled approval rather than an undocumented bypass.

concepts.name: Risk reporting
concepts.description: Risk reporting communicates material risk information to people who can make decisions. The format and detail should match the audience.

concepts.name: Business impact analysis (BIA)
concepts.description: A business impact analysis (BIA) identifies critical business functions, dependencies, and the consequences of disruption so recovery priorities can be set.

concepts.name: RTO, RPO, MTTR, and MTBF
concepts.description: Recovery metrics describe different aspects of disruption and reliability: recovery time objective (RTO) targets restoration time, recovery point objective (RPO) limits acceptable data loss measured in time, MTTR describes average repair/recovery time, and mean time between failures (MTBF) describes average operating time between failures.

concepts.name: Vendor assessment
concepts.description: Vendor assessment evaluates whether a third party's security posture and dependencies create acceptable risk before and during the relationship.

concepts.name: Right-to-audit and authorized testing
concepts.description: A right-to-audit clause preserves the customer's ability to verify agreed controls or compliance. Penetration testing must also be explicitly authorized and scoped.

concepts.name: Internal audits, independent assessments, and supply-chain analysis
concepts.description: Vendor evidence has different assurance value. Internal audit evidence comes from inside the vendor; independent assessments add external perspective; supply-chain analysis examines dependencies beyond the direct vendor.

concepts.name: Vendor selection and due diligence
concepts.description: Due diligence is the investigative work used to understand a supplier or product before making or continuing a business decision.

concepts.name: Conflict of interest
concepts.description: A conflict of interest exists when personal, financial, or organizational interests could improperly influence vendor selection or oversight.

concepts.name: Third-party agreement types
concepts.description: Security+ expects you to recognize what common agreements are for: SLA, MOA, MOU, MSA, work order/statement of work, NDA, and business partners agreement.

concepts.name: Service-level agreement (SLA)
concepts.description: A service-level agreement (SLA) defines measurable service expectations such as availability, response time, support targets, or remediation commitments.

concepts.name: MOA vs. MOU
concepts.description: A memorandum of agreement (MOA) and memorandum of understanding (MOU) both document cooperation between parties. Exact legal effect varies, so focus on the authored responsibilities and intent rather than assuming one is always legally binding.

concepts.name: MSA, work order, and statement of work
concepts.description: A master service agreement (MSA) establishes reusable relationship terms, while a work order (WO) or statement of work (SOW) defines a specific engagement, scope, deliverables, schedule, or task.

concepts.name: NDA and business partners agreement
concepts.description: A non-disclosure agreement (NDA) protects confidential information shared between parties. A business partners agreement (BPA) defines terms and responsibilities for a broader partner relationship.

concepts.name: Vendor monitoring, questionnaires, and rules of engagement
concepts.description: Third-party risk continues after onboarding. Organizations monitor vendors, request updated evidence or questionnaires, and define rules of engagement for authorized testing.

concepts.name: Internal and external compliance reporting
concepts.description: Compliance reporting communicates whether required controls, activities, or obligations are being met. Internal reports support management; external reports may support regulators, customers, partners, or auditors.

concepts.name: Consequences of non-compliance
concepts.description: Non-compliance can create financial, legal, operational, and trust consequences, including fines, sanctions, reputational damage, loss of license, and contractual impacts.

concepts.name: Due diligence and due care
concepts.description: In Security+ scenarios, due diligence is the investigation and ongoing evaluation needed to understand risk, while due care is taking reasonable protective action based on what is known.

concepts.name: Attestation and acknowledgement
concepts.description: An attestation is a formal assertion that stated conditions or requirements are true. An acknowledgement records that a person received, understood, or accepted a policy, notice, or responsibility.

concepts.name: Compliance monitoring and automation
concepts.description: Compliance monitoring checks whether obligations remain satisfied over time. It may use internal reviews, external reviews, and automation to collect evidence or detect deviations.

concepts.name: Privacy obligations across jurisdictions
concepts.description: Privacy requirements can differ across local, regional, national, and global jurisdictions. The organization must determine which legal obligations apply to its data subjects, processing, locations, and business activities.

concepts.name: Data subject, controller, and processor
concepts.description: Using common privacy terminology, the data subject is the person whose personal data is being processed, the controller determines the purposes and means of processing, and the processor handles personal data on the controller's behalf.

concepts.name: Data ownership, inventory, and retention
concepts.description: Privacy and compliance programs need a data inventory: a record of what data exists, who is accountable for it, where it is stored, and how long it should be retained.

concepts.name: Right to be forgotten / right to erasure
concepts.description: Security+ includes the right to be forgotten. In laws that provide such a right, a person may request erasure of qualifying personal data, but the right is not universal and legal exceptions can apply.

concepts.name: Attestation in audits and assessments
concepts.description: Attestation is a formal assertion or conclusion about defined subject matter. It can be supported by evidence gathered through audits or assessments, but it is not automatically the same thing as an audit.

concepts.name: Internal compliance audits and self-assessments
concepts.description: Internal audits and self-assessments are performed by or for the organization to evaluate compliance, control operation, and readiness before external review.

concepts.name: Audit committee
concepts.description: An audit committee provides governance oversight of audit, assurance, risk, and control issues rather than performing day-to-day technical administration.

concepts.name: External regulatory reviews and independent audits
concepts.description: External reviews may include regulatory examinations, assessments, or independent third-party audits. They provide evidence from outside the team operating the controls.

concepts.name: Penetration testing
concepts.description: Penetration testing is an authorized attempt to identify and exploit weaknesses to demonstrate realistic security impact within a defined scope.

concepts.name: Physical, offensive, defensive, and integrated testing
concepts.description: Security+ distinguishes physical testing from offensive, defensive, and integrated approaches. The labels describe what part of the security program the exercise emphasizes.

concepts.name: Known, partially known, and unknown environments
concepts.description: Penetration tests can provide the tester with full, partial, or minimal prior knowledge of the environment. Security+ calls these known, partially known, and unknown environments.

concepts.name: Passive vs. active reconnaissance
concepts.description: Passive reconnaissance gathers information without directly probing the target environment, while active reconnaissance interacts with target systems and is more likely to be detected.

concepts.name: Phishing awareness campaigns
concepts.description: Phishing campaigns can be used as authorized simulations to teach users how social-engineering attacks look and to measure reporting behavior.

concepts.name: Recognizing a phishing attempt
concepts.description: Phishing uses deceptive messages to push a person toward an unsafe action such as revealing credentials, approving payment, opening malicious content, or visiting a fake site.

concepts.name: Responding to reported suspicious messages
concepts.description: When a suspicious message is reported, the security process should preserve useful evidence, determine scope, contain risk when necessary, and warn or protect other users if the campaign is broader.

concepts.name: Risky, unexpected, and unintentional behavior
concepts.description: Anomalous behavior recognition helps people notice risky, unexpected, or unintentional behavior because not every security problem begins with a clearly malicious action.

concepts.name: Policies, handbooks, and situational awareness
concepts.description: User guidance turns policy into behavior people can apply in real situations. Handbooks provide reference material; situational awareness helps users recognize when context makes an action risky.

concepts.name: Insider threat, social engineering, and operational security
concepts.description: Training should cover insider-threat indicators, social-engineering pressure, and operational security (OPSEC): protecting sensitive operational details that an adversary could combine or exploit.

concepts.name: Passwords, removable media, cables, and remote work
concepts.description: Awareness training should cover everyday actions that bypass technical controls: password handling, removable media and cables, and security in hybrid or remote work environments.

concepts.name: Initial and recurring reporting and monitoring
concepts.description: Awareness programs need an initial baseline and recurring measurement so the organization can see whether behavior changes and where more training is needed.

concepts.name: Awareness program development
concepts.description: Developing an awareness program starts with business risk, audience needs, and desired behaviors rather than with a generic annual slide deck.

concepts.name: Awareness program execution and improvement
concepts.description: Execution means delivering the program, supporting reporting paths, measuring results, and revising content as threats, policies, and learner needs change.
